screens.title: The root user and sudo
screens.narratorSegment: The root user is the superuser account with UID 0 and unlimited privileges. That means root can read or write any file, change any system configuration, and create or delete any account. Because these powers can cause irreversible damage, direct root logins are often discouraged. Instead, administrators use sudo to run specific commands with elevated privileges. Sudo executes a single command as root (or another user) while logging the action. Importantly, when you invoke sudo, you enter your own password for authentication, not root's, which helps maintain an audit trail tied to the person who executed the change. A concrete example is running a package update: running the update command without sudo will fail with permission denied, while running sudo apt update allows an authorized user to update package lists. A common misconception is that sudo gives permanent root rights; it does not. Sudo grants temporary elevation for the command you run. Another trap is editing the sudoers file directly and introducing syntax errors that break sudo for all users; always use visudo which checks syntax before saving. Takeaway: prefer narrowly scoped sudo commands and keep root logins as an emergency or administrative last resort.

keyIdea.title: Why sudo?
keyIdea.text: Sudo provides controlled, auditable privilege elevation; use it instead of logging in directly as root to reduce risk and preserve accountability.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › Root and sudo
Definition and implications
  • Root has UID 0 and can perform any action; treat it as a powerful, risky account.
  • Sudo elevates a permitted user's privileges for a single command and records the action in logs.
  • Sudo authenticates using your user password, not the root password, providing traceability.
  • Use visudo to safely edit sudoers to avoid syntax mistakes that can break sudo access.
Common mistake
Relying on a single persistent root shell or giving broad sudo rights unnecessarily expands risk.
Concrete example
sudo apt update
# You will be prompted for your own password; the command runs with root privileges.
This single command showcases the pattern: the unprivileged user requests one elevated action. Logs will record who ran it and when.
Key Takeaway

Use sudo to perform targeted, auditable administrative tasks. Reserve root logins for emergencies and use visudo for safe sudoers edits.

screens.title: The identity files: /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group
screens.narratorSegment: Linux stores account and group metadata in plain-text files that form the authoritative record for identities. The first file, /etc/passwd, contains account fields such as username, a placeholder for the password field, UID, GID, the user's comment or full name, home directory, and default shell. It does not contain encrypted passwords itself. Those are stored in /etc/shadow, which holds the hashed password and password aging details. Shadow is readable only by root to protect secrets. The third file, /etc/group, lists group names, GIDs, and member lists so the system knows who belongs to each group. A key practical point is that editing these files directly can cause problems; system utilities like useradd, usermod, and groupadd update them safely. A common misconception is that passwd stores passwords; it does not. Another is thinking group membership is only primary — supplementary groups are important for permission grants. Knowing which file holds which kind of data helps you debug login and permission problems without exposing passwords or corrupting account metadata. The identity files: /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group means /etc/passwd holds account fields, /etc/shadow holds encrypted passwords, and /etc/group records group names and membership.. In practical terms, what each file stores and why access restrictions exist. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: /etc/passwd holds account fields, /etc/shadow holds encrypted passwords, and /etc/group records group names and membership.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › Identity files
File roles
/etc/passwd — Stores account fields such as username, UID, GID, home directory, and shell. The password field is a placeholder.
/etc/shadow — Stores hashed passwords and password aging data. Readable only by root.
/etc/group — Stores group names, GIDs, and a comma-separated member list for supplementary group membership.
Misconception: /etc/passwd contains passwords. In modern systems passwords live in /etc/shadow for security.
Practical examples (patterns)
Files use colon-separated fields. Use safe commands to inspect them rather than editing raw files.
# /etc/passwd pattern:
username:x:UID:GID:comment:/home/username:/bin/bash

# /etc/shadow pattern:
username:hashed-password:...:password-aging-fields

# /etc/group pattern:
groupname:x:GID:user1,user2
Key Takeaway

Inspect these files to diagnose login and membership issues, but change them with user and group utilities to avoid corruption and permission mistakes.

screens.title: Creating and deleting user accounts
screens.narratorSegment: Creating and deleting user accounts is a common administrative workflow that must be performed carefully. The standard sequence is to create an account with useradd and the -m flag to ensure a home directory is created, set a password using passwd, and verify the account with id. For example, running sudo useradd -m devuser1 creates the account and a home directory; without -m the home might be missing. Immediately following creation, run sudo passwd devuser1 to set a login password; without a password the account will not be usable for interactive login. When removing an account, the userdel command deletes the account record; adding -r will also remove the home directory and mail spool. That -r option is irreversible in ordinary practice, so always back up important user data before using it. A common mistake is creating an account but forgetting to set the password, leaving the user unable to log in, or deleting an account with -r without checking for important files. Follow the create→password→verify order and back up before destructive deletes to keep systems recoverable. Creating and deleting user accounts means create with useradd -m, set password with passwd, verify with id, and delete with userdel; use -r only when you intend to remove home data.. In practical terms, useradd, passwd, and userdel with safe flags and order of operations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Create with useradd -m, set password with passwd, verify with id, and delete with userdel; use -r only when you intend to remove home data.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › Create & Delete Users
Step-by-step process
  1. Create user with home: sudo useradd -m username
  2. Set a password: sudo passwd username
  3. Verify the account: sudo id username
  4. Delete when necessary: sudo userdel username (use -r to remove home)
Warning: userdel -r removes data. Back up before you delete.
Command examples
sudo useradd -m devuser1
sudo passwd devuser1  # set and confirm the password
sudo id devuser1

# To delete and remove home:
sudo userdel -r devuser1
Practice in a non-production environment first. Check for lingering files owned by the user before removal.
Key Takeaway

Always create the home with -m, set a password before first use, and avoid -r unless you truly want to remove home data.

screens.title: Group management and usermod flags
screens.narratorSegment: Groups let you assign permissions to multiple users at once and simplify access control. You create a group with groupadd and remove it with groupdel. Adding a user to a supplementary group is done with usermod -aG groupname username; the -a flag appends the new group to the user's existing supplementary groups. If you omit -a and only use -G, you will replace the user's supplementary group list and potentially remove them from important groups. To change a user's primary group use usermod -g primary_group username; this sets the group that will be used for new files by default. A concrete scenario: suppose you create a project_devs group and want devuser1 to participate. Run sudo groupadd project_devs, then sudo usermod -aG project_devs devuser1. Next, verify with sudo id devuser1 and look for project_devs in the groups list. A common misconception is that -G always appends; it does not. Remember the difference, and verify group membership after each change to avoid accidental permission loss. Group management and usermod flags means use usermod -ag to append supplementary groups; usermod -g replaces the supplementary group list and may remove existing memberships.. In practical terms, groupadd, groupdel, usermod -ag versus -g and changing primary groups. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Append vs replace
keyIdea.text: Use usermod -aG to append supplementary groups; usermod -G replaces the supplementary group list and may remove existing memberships.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › Group Management
Commands
sudo groupadd newgroup — create a group.
sudo groupdel oldgroup — delete a group.
sudo usermod -aG grp user — append supplementary group membership.
sudo usermod -g primary user — set primary group.
Pitfall: using -G without -a can remove existing groups unexpectedly.
Example workflow
sudo groupadd project_devs
sudo usermod -aG project_devs devuser1
sudo id devuser1  # verify project_devs appears in the groups list
Verify after each change to avoid surprises and restore quickly if you accidentally remove membership.
Pro Tip

When scripting group changes, check current membership and append rather than overwrite unless you intentionally reset groups.

screens.title: Verifying identity: whoami and id
screens.narratorSegment: Two small commands help you confirm who you are and which groups you belong to. whoami prints the effective username for the current shell, a quick check when you need to confirm privilege. The id command is more informative: it shows the UID, primary GID, and all supplementary groups for the current or a specified user. For example, id cohortiauser will reveal numeric IDs and named groups. Use these commands after changing memberships or when debugging 'permission denied' errors. A concrete example is adding a user to project_devs and then running id to ensure the new group appears; if it doesn't, the user may need to log out and back in or you may have used the wrong usermod flags. A misconception is trusting only file ownership during troubleshooting; group membership also controls access through group permissions. Practice reading id output: numbers identify system-level IDs while names are easier for humans. Closing question: when you see a process running as root, what does whoami and id tell you about how that process acquired its privileges? content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › Verify identity
Quick checks
Run these commands to confirm the current effective user and its IDs.
whoami
# prints the current effective username

id
# prints uid, gid, and all groups for the current user

id cohortiauser
# prints uid, gid, and groups for the specified user
If you add a user to a group and the group does not appear in id, the user session may need to be restarted or the usermod command may have been used incorrectly.
Reading id output
  • uid=1001(username) shows numeric uid and name.
  • gid=1001(groupname) shows the primary group.
  • groups=1001(groupname),1002(other) lists supplementary group membership.
Check Your Understanding

After adding a user to a group, what two steps might you take if id does not show the new group?

screens.title: Sudoers file and visudo safety
screens.narratorSegment: The sudoers file determines which users may run which commands as root or other users. Editing this file incorrectly can prevent all users from gaining elevated rights, so never edit it with a plain editor. Instead, use visudo; it locks the file and performs syntax checking before saving, reducing the risk of syntax errors that break sudo. Apply the principle of least privilege when granting sudo rights: prefer allowing specific commands rather than giving blanket root access. For example, permit a user to restart a service or run package management commands without granting full shell access as root. A common misconception is that wide sudo rights simplify administration; in fact they expand the attack surface. Always document sudo rules and test them for the intended scope. If you must grant temporary access, remove it when tasks are complete. This combination of careful editing, minimal privilege, and regular review keeps sudo safe and maintains accountability in multi-admin environments. Sudoers file and visudo safety means use visudo to edit sudoers and follow least privilege: grant only the specific commands users need.. In practical terms, why edit sudoers with care and how the principle of least privilege guides sudo configuration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Switching users with su and session considerations
screens.narratorSegment: At times you'll need to operate as another user to verify their environment or simulate their permissions. screens.title: Walkthrough: Basic user and group management lab
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough follows the lab sequence from the chapter and ties each command to its purpose. Start by checking your current identity with whoami and id to confirm the environment. Inspect /etc/passwd with head -n 5 to see account field patterns. Create a group with sudo groupadd project_devs; this defines a shared identity for project members. Then create a user with sudo useradd -m devuser1; the -m makes the home directory. Immediately set a password with sudo passwd devuser1 so the account can log in. Add the user to the project group using sudo usermod -aG project_devs devuser1; the -a avoids removing other memberships. Verify with sudo id devuser1 to ensure project_devs appears in the group list. To test the user environment, su - devuser1 and rerun id; then exit to return. When you finish, remove the user and their home directory with sudo userdel -r devuser1, then remove the group with sudo groupdel project_devs. Finally, verify deletions with grep project_devs /etc/group and id devuser1; both should indicate absence. Throughout, back up any important data before deletion and never reuse example passwords in production.

Step sequence and commands
# Check current user and ids
whoami
id

# View account patterns
head -n 5 /etc/passwd

# Create group and verify
sudo groupadd project_devs
grep project_devs /etc/group

# Create user, set password, add to group
sudo useradd -m devuser1
sudo passwd devuser1
sudo usermod -aG project_devs devuser1

su - devuser1
id
exit

sudo groupdel project_devs

Work through each step in a safe lab. Use simple exercise passwords here, but never reuse them in production. Back up data before any destructive commands.

Follow the ordered sequence and verify membership and identity at each step to avoid mistakes and keep a recoverable workflow.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will build a clear mental model of how Linux uses users and groups to control access. We'll explain the special role of the root user, why sudo is the safer way to perform administrative work, and how the system stores account and group information in three core files. You will also encounter the basic commands administrators use every day: adding and removing users and groups, setting passwords, and managing group membership. By the end you'll understand not just the commands, but the why: why root is restricted, why passwords belong in shadow rather than passwd, and why the principle of least privilege matters for system safety. For example, you will see how creating a project group and adding developers to it makes permission management simpler than changing individual file permissions repeatedly. We'll also surface common errors to avoid, such as forgetting to use sudo or accidentally deleting a home directory. Start with curiosity: ask yourself which accounts really need admin rights and how you can limit that exposure.

By the end of the chapter you will be able to identify and explain the roles of users and groups in Linux, including the special root account and the security reasons to avoid direct root logins. You will also be able to locate and describe the purpose of the three key system files that store identity and group information. Practically, you will create and remove user accounts and groups on the command line, set passwords, and safely add users to supplementary groups. Finally, you will use sudo correctly to run administrative commands and apply basic security practices such as enforcing strong passwords and following the principle of least privilege. Each objective emphasizes both the command syntax and the operational reasoning behind it. For example, creating a project group and adding developers to it is both a command exercise and a permissions design decision that reduces administrative complexity. These objectives prepare you to perform typical administration tasks while reducing risk to the system.

This second objectives slide focuses on practical verification and safety. You will learn to verify identity and group membership using whoami and id, and to inspect the first lines of /etc/passwd to confirm account fields. You will practice adding a group, creating a user with a home directory, setting a password, and adding that user to the group using usermod with the append flag. You will also learn the difference between replacing and appending group memberships, a small syntax detail with large consequences. Finally, you will practice safe cleanup: deleting a user and optionally removing their home directory, while understanding when data removal is irreversible. These exercises build command fluency and a cautious mindset so you can administer systems without accidentally removing important files or granting excessive rights. Learning Objectives — Continued means practice verification with whoami and id, create users and groups, and learn safe cleanup and membership management techniques.. In practical terms, practical commands, verification, and safety checks. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The root user is the superuser account with UID 0 and unlimited privileges. That means root can read or write any file, change any system configuration, and create or delete any account. Because these powers can cause irreversible damage, direct root logins are often discouraged. Instead, administrators use sudo to run specific commands with elevated privileges. Sudo executes a single command as root (or another user) while logging the action. Importantly, when you invoke sudo, you enter your own password for authentication, not root's, which helps maintain an audit trail tied to the person who executed the change. A concrete example is running a package update: running the update command without sudo will fail with permission denied, while running sudo apt update allows an authorized user to update package lists. A common misconception is that sudo gives permanent root rights; it does not. Sudo grants temporary elevation for the command you run. Another trap is editing the sudoers file directly and introducing syntax errors that break sudo for all users; always use visudo which checks syntax before saving. Takeaway: prefer narrowly scoped sudo commands and keep root logins as an emergency or administrative last resort.

Linux stores account and group metadata in plain-text files that form the authoritative record for identities. The first file, /etc/passwd, contains account fields such as username, a placeholder for the password field, UID, GID, the user's comment or full name, home directory, and default shell. It does not contain encrypted passwords itself. Those are stored in /etc/shadow, which holds the hashed password and password aging details. Shadow is readable only by root to protect secrets. The third file, /etc/group, lists group names, GIDs, and member lists so the system knows who belongs to each group. A key practical point is that editing these files directly can cause problems; system utilities like useradd, usermod, and groupadd update them safely. A common misconception is that passwd stores passwords; it does not. Another is thinking group membership is only primary — supplementary groups are important for permission grants. Knowing which file holds which kind of data helps you debug login and permission problems without exposing passwords or corrupting account metadata. The identity files: /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group means /etc/passwd holds account fields, /etc/shadow holds encrypted passwords, and /etc/group records group names and membership.. In practical terms, what each file stores and why access restrictions exist. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Creating and deleting user accounts is a common administrative workflow that must be performed carefully. The standard sequence is to create an account with useradd and the -m flag to ensure a home directory is created, set a password using passwd, and verify the account with id. For example, running sudo useradd -m devuser1 creates the account and a home directory; without -m the home might be missing. Immediately following creation, run sudo passwd devuser1 to set a login password; without a password the account will not be usable for interactive login. When removing an account, the userdel command deletes the account record; adding -r will also remove the home directory and mail spool. That -r option is irreversible in ordinary practice, so always back up important user data before using it. A common mistake is creating an account but forgetting to set the password, leaving the user unable to log in, or deleting an account with -r without checking for important files. Groups let you assign permissions to multiple users at once and simplify access control. You create a group with groupadd and remove it with groupdel.
